title: Spectral projections: selecting whole pieces of an operator
subtitle: G2 lecture 030000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: Individual eigenvalues of a self-adjoint matrix can be ordered and compared using Rayleigh quotients and min-max characterizations.
body: But many perturbation questions concern an entire selected collection of eigendirections rather than any one eigenvector. But the Davis–Kahan theory that motivates this course is often not interested in one eigenvector at a time. It asks how a subspace associated with a group of eigenvalues behaves. To prepare for that question, we need a way to say: keep the part of a vector associated with these eigenvalues, and discard everything else.

slides.title: Selecting frequencies in a simple analogy
body: It contains several pitches mixed together. If we could separate the chord into its pitch components, we might choose to keep only the notes above a certain frequency. For a self-adjoint matrix, the finite spectral theorem gives an exact decomposition of every vector into orthogonal components belonging to distinct eigenvalues. We can select some of those components and suppress the others. The analogy is imperfect: an eigenvalue need not be a frequency, and an operator need not describe sound. But the operation of selecting components is precisely the same kind of bookkeeping. Let's build it from the eigenbasis rather than starting with a formula to memorize.

slides.title: The projector for one eigenspace
body: Pick one of its eigenvalues, say lambda. All the vectors that A multiplies by lambda form the corresponding eigenspace. Because the space is finite-dimensional, there is an orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. Call it P lambda. Applying P lambda to a vector keeps the component in that eigenspace and removes all perpendicular components. If we apply P lambda twice, the second application changes nothing. That is the defining behavior of a projection. If we take its adjoint, we get the same operator, because this is an orthogonal projection. What happens if we project onto one eigenspace, then onto an eigenspace for a different eigenvalue? The result is zero.

slides.title: Selecting a set of eigenvalues
slides.lead: Now choose any set S of real numbers.
body: It might be a finite list, a closed interval, an open interval, or all numbers above a threshold. For each eigenvalue belonging to S, keep its spectral projection. Add those projections together. Ignore the eigenvalues outside S. The resulting operator is the spectral projection of A onto S. The set S itself can contain numbers that are not eigenvalues. Those extra numbers have no effect: there is no eigenspace component for them to select. To calculate this projection on a vector, decompose the vector into eigenspace components, keep exactly the ones whose eigenvalues lie in S, and add them back together.

slides.title: A calculation we can hear
slides.lead: Consider the symmetric two-by-two matrix with rows two, one and one, two.
body: We have used it before. Its eigenvalues are three and one. Its eigenvectors lie along the lines one, one and one, negative one. Suppose S contains all real numbers greater than two. Only the eigenvalue three is selected. Projection onto its normalized eigenvector produces a matrix with one-half in each of its four entries. Apply that projection to the vector with coordinates four and zero. We get the vector two, two. The component along the diagonal line is preserved; the perpendicular component is removed. Now select the interval from zero through two instead.

slides.title: Why endpoints matter
slides.lead: Now imagine a selection rule that keeps eigenvalues greater than or equal to one.
body: Our matrix has an eigenvalue exactly equal to one, so it is included. The projector is the identity. Change just one word: keep eigenvalues strictly greater than one. Now the eigenspace for one is excluded, and only the eigenspace for three remains. The difference between a closed and an open interval can therefore change the selected spectral subspace immediately when an eigenvalue lies on the boundary. If we move a threshold through a region containing no eigenvalues, the projection does not change at all.

slides.title: What if an eigenvalue repeats?
slides.lead: Suppose A has diagonal entries four, four, and one.
body: The eigenspace for four is a plane, and the eigenspace for one is a line perpendicular to it. Selecting eigenvalue four keeps the entire plane. The spectral projection has diagonal entries one, one, and zero. Could we instead select just one of the two coordinate axes in that plane? We could certainly project onto that line. Since A acts as four times the identity on the whole plane, the line projection would even commute with A. But it would not be a spectral projection defined by a set of eigenvalues. The selection rule cannot distinguish two directions that carry exactly the same eigenvalue.

slides.title: Why a spectral projection commutes with the operator
body: Split it into its selected spectral components and its unselected spectral components. If we first apply the projection and then apply A, each selected component gets multiplied by its eigenvalue. If we first apply A and then project, A multiplies every spectral component by its eigenvalue, but the projection removes the unselected ones afterward. The same selected components survive with the same multipliers in either order. Therefore the spectral projection commutes with A. That means its range is invariant under A, and so is its perpendicular complement. By definition, a spectral subspace is a reducing subspace.

slides.title: Combining selections
slides.lead: The selection rules obey simple algebra.
body: Selecting S and then selecting T is the same as selecting their intersection, because a component survives both steps exactly when its eigenvalue belongs to both sets. If S and T are disjoint, their selected subspaces are orthogonal and the projection for their union is the sum of their projections. Selecting the complement of S keeps everything that S discarded, so its projection is the identity minus the projection for S. These identities are useful because they let us manipulate spectral regions using operators, without returning to coordinates after every step.

slides.title: Spectral selection as an operator function
slides.lead: Spectral selection is an example of applying a function to a self-adjoint operator.
body: The indicator of a set S takes the value one on S and zero outside S. Applied to a finite-dimensional self-adjoint matrix through its eigenvalue decomposition, this indicator produces the corresponding spectral projection. For an infinite-dimensional self-adjoint operator, the spectrum need not consist of isolated eigenvalues. A projection-valued spectral measure gives the correct extension of the indicator construction to that setting; the finite eigenbasis argument alone does not establish it. For now, try reconstructing the two-by-two example.

slides.title: The mathematical relationship
slides.lead: Spectral selection is an example of applying a function to a self-adjoint operator.
body: The indicator of a set S takes the value one on S and zero outside S. Applied to a finite-dimensional self-adjoint matrix through its eigenvalue decomposition, this indicator produces the corresponding spectral projection.

slides.title: What to retain
slides.lead: Its projector commutes with the self-adjoint operator, and repeated eigenvalues must be selected together when the selection is made solely by eigenvalue.
